title: Reaching Inside One Living Cell
endLine: Move molecules, nuclei, or cytoplasm into living cells to test cause.

scenes.tts: How do you test what drives a living cell from inside? Watching from outside shows events happening together, not cause. To test cause directly, place a molecule, nucleus, or cytoplasm straight inside one cell.
scenes.caption: How do you test what drives a living cell from inside? Watching from outside shows events happening together, not cause. To test cause directly, place a molecule, nucleus, or cytoplasm straight inside one cell.
scenes.visual: Schematic microscope-stage view filling most of the frame: one intact living cell with a glowing nucleus inside a gently drifting cytoplasm. The opening question appears above the cell; as the third sentence speaks, a fine glass needle glides in from the right while a glowing dot, a spare nucleus, and a neighbouring cell highlight in turn.
scenes.narration: How do you test what drives a living cell from inside? Watching from outside shows events happening together, not cause. To test cause directly, place a molecule, nucleus, or cytoplasm straight inside one cell.

scenes.visual: Title card 'Reaching Inside One Living Cell' fades over the softly drifting living cell on the same schematic stage, then clears cleanly.

scenes.tts: Start with microinjection. A fine glass needle pierces one cell, placing a molecule into its cytoplasm, outside the nucleus. That skips the steps outside the cell and tests what that molecule does inside. A marker dye rides along to identify every injected cell.
scenes.caption: Start with microinjection. A fine glass needle pierces one cell, placing a molecule into its cytoplasm, outside the nucleus. That skips the steps outside the cell and tests what that molecule does inside. A marker dye rides along to identify every injected cell.
scenes.visual: Same schematic cell and stage. The fine glass needle advances into the membrane and releases a bright puff of dots (no molecular structures) into the cytoplasm around the nucleus, bypassing faded outside signals. A soft coloured marker dye spreads through the injected cell so it stands out from an uninjected neighbour.
scenes.narration: Start with microinjection. A fine glass needle pierces one cell, placing a molecule into its cytoplasm, outside the nucleus. That skips the steps outside the cell and tests what that molecule does inside. A marker dye rides along to identify every injected cell.

scenes.tts: Other questions need more than one molecule. In nuclear transfer, you remove or destroy an egg's own nucleus and place another cell's nucleus inside. In cell fusion, you merge two cells so two nuclei share one cytoplasm. All three share one rule: put a part inside a living cell to test what it drives.
scenes.caption: Other questions need more than one molecule. In nuclear transfer, you remove or destroy an egg's own nucleus and place another cell's nucleus inside. In cell fusion, you merge two cells so two nuclei share one cytoplasm. All three share one rule: put a part inside a living cell to test what it drives.
scenes.visual: Same schematic stage. First the cell scales smoothly into a large egg: its original nucleus vanishes and the glass needle inserts a brightly coloured donor nucleus. Next, back at cell scale, two cells drift together and their membranes merge into one cell holding two distinct nuclei in one shared cytoplasm.
scenes.narration: Other questions need more than one molecule. In nuclear transfer, you remove or destroy an egg's own nucleus and place another cell's nucleus inside. In cell fusion, you merge two cells so two nuclei share one cytoplasm. All three share one rule: put a part inside a living cell to test what it drives.

scenes.tts: Now test how to read a result. Suppose you put a tadpole gut nucleus into an egg whose own nucleus was destroyed. Most eggs fail to develop, and only a small fraction become normal tadpoles. Do those failures show specialized nuclei had discarded developmental genes?
scenes.caption: Now test how to read a result. Suppose you put a tadpole gut nucleus into an egg whose own nucleus was destroyed. Most eggs fail to develop, and only a small fraction become normal tadpoles. Do those failures show specialized nuclei had discarded developmental genes?
scenes.visual: Same schematic stage zooms slightly out to show a dish of transferred eggs. A donor gut nucleus enters an emptied egg; most eggs stall and dim while a small fraction develop into swimming tadpoles. The predict question appears clearly above the dish.
scenes.narration: Now test how to read a result. Suppose you put a tadpole gut nucleus into an egg whose own nucleus was destroyed. Most eggs fail to develop, and only a small fraction become normal tadpoles. Do those failures show specialized nuclei had discarded developmental genes?

scenes.visual: The predict question remains on screen over the schematic dish of stalled eggs beside one swimming tadpole while a quiet schematic timer bar glides smoothly along the bottom.

scenes.tts: No. Failures alone cannot show what was missing. Each normal tadpole shows that specialized nucleus kept the needed instructions, and egg cytoplasm could read them. A genetic nuclear marker rules out a surviving egg nucleus. Still, low success left doubt that successes came from rare unspecialized cells.

scenes.visual: Same schematic dish. The swimming tadpole brightens as the failed eggs dim; a clear tag on its nucleus marks the donor genetic marker, ruling out the original egg nucleus. A small schematic callout notes the rare-unspecialized-cell doubt beside the low fraction of survivors.

scenes.tts: Cell fusion needs its own controls, because merging cells might itself trigger or block a response. Pre-labelling one partner with a nuclear dye identifies every nucleus inside the fused cell. Same-phase fusions and unfused neighbours on the same slide test whether fusion itself changes anything.
scenes.caption: Cell fusion needs its own controls, because merging cells might itself trigger or block a response. Pre-labelling one partner with a nuclear dye identifies every nucleus inside the fused cell. Same-phase fusions and unfused neighbours on the same slide test whether fusion itself changes anything.
scenes.visual: Same schematic stage returns to cell fusion. Before two cells merge, one partner's nucleus lights up with a pre-applied dye so both nuclei stay identifiable after fusion. Beside the mixed fused pair, schematic same-phase fused pairs and an unfused neighbour sit on the same slide.
scenes.narration: Cell fusion needs its own controls, because merging cells might itself trigger or block a response. Pre-labelling one partner with a nuclear dye identifies every nucleus inside the fused cell. Same-phase fusions and unfused neighbours on the same slide test whether fusion itself changes anything.

scenes.tts: With controls in place, these methods unlocked three landmark discoveries. In 1962 at Oxford, John Gurdon put tadpole intestinal nuclei into Xenopus laevis frog eggs lacking nuclei. A small fraction became normal feeding tadpoles, nervous system included. The gut-cell nucleus still held instructions for a whole animal.

scenes.visual: Same schematic stage with a '1962 — John Gurdon' label. A nucleus from a schematic tadpole gut lining enters an emptied frog egg, which transforms smoothly into a feeding tadpole with a glowing nervous system.

scenes.tts: Second, in 1970 Rao and Johnson fused cultured HeLa cells from different phases, sharing one cytoplasm. Beside an S phase cell copying D N A, an uncopied G one nucleus started replicating early. A copied G two nucleus did not. As later reviews describe, S phase cytoplasm can start replication. Under these fusion conditions a replicated nucleus did not.
scenes.caption: Second, in 1970 Rao and Johnson fused cultured HeLa cells from different phases, sharing one cytoplasm. Beside an S-phase cell copying DNA, an uncopied G1 nucleus started replicating early. A copied G2 nucleus did not. As later reviews describe, S-phase cytoplasm can start replication. Under these fusion conditions a replicated nucleus did not.
scenes.visual: Same schematic stage with a '1970 — Rao and Johnson' label. Two schematic pairs fuse on the slide: on the left, a G1 nucleus paired with an actively pulsing S-phase cell lights up and starts copying; on the right, a G2 nucleus paired with an S-phase cell stays quiet.
scenes.narration: Second, in 1970 Rao and Johnson fused cultured HeLa cells from different phases, sharing one cytoplasm. Beside an S-phase cell copying DNA, an uncopied G1 nucleus started replicating early. A copied G2 nucleus did not. As later reviews describe, S-phase cytoplasm can start replication. Under these fusion conditions a replicated nucleus did not.

scenes.tts: Third, in 1992 Anne Ridley and Alan Hall injected purified proteins into serum-starved fibroblasts. Those cells start with few stress fibres. Active Rho filled them with thick actin cables, while active Rac made their edges ruffle. Putting molecules, nuclei, or cytoplasm straight into living cells shows what controls each response.

Two schematic serum-starved fibroblasts with smooth interiors receive needle injections (no molecular structures): the Rho-injected cell fills with bold internal actin cables, while the Rac-injected cell develops rippling, ruffled edges.
